programs.title: Prince of Persia
programs.subtitle: Apple II, 1989
programs.author: Jordan Mechner
programs.description: The game that invented cinematic platformers — built by one developer over four years on Apple II hardware with 128K of RAM. The source code was recovered in 2012 from 22-year-old floppy disks.

files.title: SOUND.S
files.description: The complete sound engine — twenty sounds, one speaker, zero compromises

files.title: BOOT.S
files.description: The two-stage disk boot loader with 128K memory check

files.title: SEQTABLE.S
files.description: The animation state machine — every movement rotoscoped from film

files.title: MASTER.S
files.description: Game flow controller: boot, attract mode, save/load, level sequencing

programs.introduction:
In 1985, Jordan Mechner, a young programmer and aspiring filmmaker, sat down at his Apple II computer in his parents’ home in Chappaqua, New York, to begin work on what would become one of the most influential video games of all time. At the age of 21, fresh off the success of his first game, *Karateka*, Mechner was determined to push the boundaries of what a computer game could achieve. He envisioned a game that would combine fluid, lifelike animation with a gripping narrative, creating an experience that felt more like a movie than a traditional arcade game. Over the next four years, Mechner would pour his creativity, technical skill, and sheer determination into crafting *Prince of Persia*, a groundbreaking cinematic platformer that would redefine the genre.

The computing world of the mid-1980s was a place of severe constraints and ingenious solutions. The Apple II, released in 1977, was still a popular platform, but its hardware was aging rapidly in the face of newer, more powerful machines like the Commodore Amiga and IBM PC. The Apple IIe, the model Mechner used, had a mere 128K of RAM and relied on the 6502 microprocessor, a chip with just 3,510 transistors and no built-in multiplication or division instructions. Every byte of memory was precious, and developers had to squeeze every ounce of performance from the hardware. Mechner embraced these limitations, using techniques like bank-switched memory and hand-optimized assembly code to fit his ambitious vision into the confines of the Apple II.

Mechner’s background as both a programmer and a filmmaker shaped the game’s development. To create the prince’s fluid movements, he turned to rotoscoping, a technique borrowed from animation. He filmed his younger brother, David, performing acrobatic moves like running, jumping, and climbing, then traced each frame by hand to create lifelike animations. “I wanted the prince to move like a human being, not like a robot,” Mechner later recalled. This painstaking process resulted in some of the most realistic character animations ever seen in a video game at the time. Mechner also wrote every line of the game’s code himself, crafting modules for collision detection, physics, sound, and game flow, all while juggling the constraints of the Apple II’s limited hardware.

The final product, released in 1989, was nothing short of revolutionary. *Prince of Persia* combined fluid animation, tight controls, and a sense of cinematic drama that had never been seen in a platformer. Players guided the prince through treacherous dungeons filled with traps, enemies, and puzzles, all while racing against a ticking clock to rescue the princess. The game’s innovative design and storytelling captivated players and critics alike, earning it widespread acclaim and spawning ports to nearly every major platform of the era. It also laid the foundation for the cinematic platformer genre, influencing countless games that followed.

Decades later, the legacy of *Prince of Persia* endures. The source code, long thought lost, was recovered in 2012 from a set of 22-year-old floppy disks, allowing fans and historians to study the inner workings of this landmark game. Mechner’s creation not only reshaped the video game industry but also demonstrated the power of individual creativity in the face of technical limitations. Today, *Prince of Persia* is remembered as a masterpiece of design and innovation, a testament to what one person can achieve with vision, perseverance, and a willingness to push boundaries.

programs.title: Zork
programs.subtitle: PDP-10 / ITS, 1977–1979
programs.author: Anderson, Blank, Daniels, Lebling
programs.description: The game that invented the text adventure — built organically at MIT on a PDP-10, recovered from a 1990 tape, and released open-source in 2025. Its parser, its puzzles, and its sarcastic error messages changed computing forever.

files.title: defs.63
files.description: The complete type system — ROOM, OBJECT, SYNTAX, and the parser data structures

files.title: np.93
files.description: The 93rd version of the natural language parser

files.title: dung.56
files.description: The world itself — every room, exit, and object in the dungeon

files.title: act1.38
files.description: Game loop, action handlers, and the real access-control guard

programs.title: MS-DOS
programs.subtitle: IBM PC, 1981–1983
programs.author: Tim Paterson / Microsoft
programs.description: Written in six weeks by one programmer, acquired by Microsoft for $25,000, and licensed to IBM — then to every IBM clone maker on earth. The source code of the PC era.

files.title: MSDOS.ASM
files.description: The original 86-DOS kernel — Tim Paterson's byline and a revision history written in assembly comments

files.title: COMMAND.ASM
files.description: The command interpreter — 'Abort, Retry, Ignore?' in its original form

files.title: XENIX.ASM
files.description: The Unix layer that gave DOS subdirectories, pipes, and file handles

files.title: MSCODE.ASM
files.description: The v2.0 kernel — the INT 21h dispatcher and a comment that says 'Here comes multitasking!!!'

files.title: SYSINIT.ASM
files.description: The boot sequence — memory sizing, CONFIG.SYS parsing, and the launch of COMMAND.COM

files.title: FAT.ASM
files.description: The FAT filesystem — the file allocation table that outlasted DOS by decades

files.title: EXEC.ASM
files.description: Program loader — how DOS launches and returns from .COM and .EXE files
